name: Felix Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not linked to AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive ten minutes to a unit on the business park, where four of us work for a small agency. Most of our money comes from one housing developer, so I spend my days on brochures for new estates, site boards, the big printed fences round building sites, and the odd estate agent's window card. I like InDesign, I like a tidy grid, and I like it when nobody changes the plan halfway through.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Changes, mostly. The developer will move a show home and we redo forty pages. And money: I rent a room above the hardware shop, I've got about a fortnight's money in the bank, and I'm on the low end for designers. There's one other agency in town, and they're not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I never used it anyway. I'd say it at the Friday pub with Martin, my boss, and the lads. Online I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but my real worry stays the same. One developer pays most of our bills, and if house building slows down, we slow down. Half our agency's money comes from one housing developer, so a slow year for house building worries me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd try to save a bit more, maybe sixty a month, and I'd keep my car running another year instead of replacing it. Maybe I'd ask Martin about learning the web side, but probably not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. A bit of the usual low hum about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said probably not, about the web side. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not great at new software, if I'm honest. I took two months to feel right in InDesign. I'd rather be good at one thing than bad at three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the developer cut back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin would probably cut hours before cutting people, so I'd go to four days. Four days' pay doesn't cover the rent and the car, so I'd be asking my dad for help, which I hate.

say: I'd say **fine by me**, I never used AI anyway.
I'd say it at the **Friday pub**, not online.
think: Our real risk is relying on **one housing developer**.
If building slows, I'd likely drop to **four days** a week.
do: Keep working **as I am** on brochures and site boards.
Keep the **old car** running another year.
feel: **Relieved**, with the usual **low hum** about money underneath.
S0.quote: Half our agency's money comes from one housing developer, so a slow year for house building worries me more than any robot.
fieldNote: His concern is **client concentration**, not technology.
He avoids learning new software, preferring to be **good at one thing**.
His fallback is **his dad**, which he dislikes.

steps.text: Keep doing brochures and site boards the same way
Save sixty more a month toward a cushion
Keep the old car running another year instead of replacing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is what it is. Some jobs go, some come, that's always been true. I wouldn't blame anyone, it's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm probably in trouble. The developer could get brochure layouts out of a machine and just pay a printer. If the developer asks why they're paying our agency for brochures a machine can lay out, I don't know what Martin (his boss) would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on and see what Martin does first. If he starts using it, I'd have to learn it, I know that. I'd also talk to my dad about the electrician apprenticeship he's always on at me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into anxious. Like waiting for a phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what Martin does. What if he's waiting for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Maybe. Martin's fifty-eight and he hates new software more than I do. That's the only reason I'm not more worried, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I told you so, then he'd ring his mate who runs a firm. Electricians fit things in walls and lofts, that's not a computer's job anytime soon. I just don't know if I'd be any good at it.

say: I'd say **it is** what it is; jobs come and go.
I wouldn't **blame anyone**, because it's just business.
think: The developer could get **layouts from a machine** and only pay a printer.
Martin's own **dislike of software** is my only real cover.
do: **Wait** to see whether Martin brings in the tools.
Learn the **AI tools** only if Martin makes me.
Talk to my dad about an **electrician apprenticeship**.
feel: **Uneasy** turning to **anxious**, like waiting for a call.
S1.quote: If the developer asks why they're paying our agency for brochures a machine can lay out, I don't know what Martin (his boss) would say.
fieldNote: He waits on his **boss's choices** rather than his own.
His safety rests on a **reluctant older boss**, which he sees clearly.
The **electrician route** is a family-backed, hands-on fallback.

steps.text: Wait to see whether Martin (his boss) adopts AI tools
Ask his dad's electrician friend about an apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's mad, nobody's ready. I'd say the government should slow it down. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the design job's gone. Brochures, boards, everything I do is on a screen, so 2028 is the end of it. The building sites still need electricians until around 2031, and probably longer in old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad's mate and start the apprenticeship as soon as he'd take me, even at apprentice pay. I'd give up the room and move back home to afford it. I'd sell the car and use dad's van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Starting again at 27 when I only just got started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Apprentice pay is low. How would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't, without my parents. I'd be 27, starting an electrician apprenticeship, sleeping on my parents' sofa bed, and the robots would be three years behind me. My mum would be pleased, my dad would be smug, and I'd be on the sofa bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2031, when robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know. I'd hope old houses are too awkward for robots for a while. But I'd be lying if I said I had a plan for that.

say: I'd say it's **mad**, because nobody's ready, not firms and not families.
I'd ask the government to **slow it down** before it hits.
think: Everything I do is on a screen, so **2028 ends** my design job.
Electricians are needed until about **2031**, longer in old houses.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** as soon as possible.
Give up the room and **move back home**.
**Sell the car** and borrow dad's van.
S2.quote: I'd be 27, starting an electrician apprenticeship, sleeping on my parents' sofa bed, and the robots would be three years behind me.
fieldNote: He'd switch to a **hands-on trade** fast, but only with **family help**.
The **three-year robot gap** is his whole plan.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship with his dad's friend's firm
Give up the rented room and move back to his parents
Sell the car and borrow his dad's van
Lean on his parents for food and rent while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so people should use them. I'd say it in a calm way, I don't like shouting about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the same end, just later. My design work goes around 2030 maybe, and robots come 2034. Five years means I could finish an apprenticeship before AGI and have a few years as a qualified electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency one more year and save hard, maybe a hundred a month. Then I'd start the apprenticeship. I'd keep the car this time, I'd need it for jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's not a cliff. More like a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't like learning new things. Does a trade feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, because you can see it. A wire's connected or it isn't. Software keeps changing every six months, but a wire is either connected or it isn't, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Martin when you left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd thank him and say I saw it coming. He'd probably say he's retiring anyway. He's got a caravan he keeps talking about.

say: I'd say people should **use the few years** they've got.
I'd say it **calmly** at the pub, not shouting online.
think: My screen-based design work likely goes around **2030**, before AGI.
Five years lets me **qualify as an electrician** before AGI.
do: Stay at the agency **one more year** and save hard.
Save about **a hundred a month** first.
feel: **Worried**, but it's a **steep hill**, not a cliff.
S3.quote: Software keeps changing every six months, but a wire is either connected or it isn't, and I like that.
fieldNote: He frames the trade as **stable and visible**, which suits his dislike of change.
Five years turns a panic move into a **planned switch**.
He still expects to **lose design work** entirely.

steps.text: Stay one more year at the agency and save a hundred a month
Start an electrician apprenticeship after that year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most of us will be fine if we're sensible. I'd tell my mates not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd probably keep designing for a good few years. Martin retires, maybe the agency closes, and I'd move on before 2036 anyway. Ten years means I could get properly qualified in something hands-on without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the agency for now. I'd do an evening electrics course in a couple of years, just to have it. I'd see what happens with the developer before making a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far off, but I know it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's my problem. Give me ten years and I'll spend nine of them putting it off, because I never move until I have to. My dad would keep nagging me, which would probably help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else you'd change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait before moving in with my girlfriend, Lena. Not because of her, because I'd want to know what I'm earning in five years.

say: I'd say ten years is long; most people will be fine if **sensible**.
I'd tell my mates **not to panic**.
think: I'd keep designing for **a few more years**.
Ten years lets me **qualify in a trade** without rushing.
do: Keep working at the agency **for now**.
Do an evening **electrics course** in two years.
Wait on the **developer contract** before a big jump.
feel: **Uneasy**, because it's **far off** but definitely coming.
S4.quote: Give me ten years and I'll spend nine of them putting it off, because I never move until I have to.
fieldNote: He knows his **habit of delay** is the real risk here.
His job still **ends before 2036**, so he isn't secure.
He'd **delay moving in** with his girlfriend until income is clear.

steps.text: Keep designing at the agency while the developer contract lasts
Take an evening electrics course in two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be on my parents' sofa learning a trade from scratch. What would help is apprentice pay you can live on, maybe topped up by the government, so you don't need your parents to bail you out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many of us there are. Every town has a few designers like me who are fine at a grid and not much else, and nobody's thinking about where we go.

headlineQuote: Every town has a few designers like me who are fine at a grid and not much else, and nobody's thinking about where we go.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old junior** designer doing brochures and site boards for a housing developer.
He **never uses AI**, avoids new software, and rents a room with a fortnight's savings.
He's pragmatic, doesn't **blame anyone**, and waits for his boss to move first.
His fallback is an **electrician apprenticeship** through his dad.
His mood climbs from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as AI gets faster.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be starting a trade from scratch on his parents' sofa.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprentice pay** you can live on, topped up by **government**.
